::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Shortest distance between two points](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3444463/shortest-distance-between-two-points), asked by [mulaffar abdullah](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/719159/mulaffar-abdullah) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2019-11-21; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Everyone knows that the shortest distance between two points is a straight line. How can we prove it mathematically?
:::

If $y$ is a $C^2$ function of $x$ and traces a curve between points $(a,c)$ and $(b,d)$, then the length of the curve is 
$$\ell = \int_a^b \sqrt{1+(y')^2}\,dx$$
This is the kind of functional that we can apply the [calculus of variations][1] to.  According the Euler-Lagrange equations (see link), the quantity $\ell$ is minimized when
$$\frac{d}{dx} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'}\sqrt{1+(y')^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\sqrt{1+(y')^2}$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{y'}{\sqrt{1+(y')^2}} = 0
    \implies \frac{y''}{(1+(y')^2)^{3/2}} = 0
    \implies y'' = 0$$
If $y'' = 0$, the curve is a straight line.


  [1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus_of_variations
